I am a 55-year-old woman farming in Quzhou. I never went to school, but I have been farming this land since I was young. My family has about 6 mu of good flat land, and we have a reliable well for irrigation. 

My wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October, as we always do. The start of the growing season now means I need to manage it through to harvest. I will not gamble with strange crops. Everyone around me grows wheat in winter and maize in summer; that is what the land is for, and that is what the buyers come for. My husband passed away a few years ago, and my son works in the city, so I manage most of the field work myself with some hired help at harvest. 

For the wheat, I will use an improved variety like Jimai 22 — it is what the seed shop recommends and what my neighbors plant. I will put down urea at greening and jointing, and I have already applied compound fertilizer as basal last autumn. I will irrigate four times: winter water, greening water, jointing water, and grain-filling water. That is what my father taught me, and it works. For pests, I will spray herbicide once in spring, and if I see rust or aphids, I will add fungicide or insecticide. I till with rotary tillage before sowing.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize — Denghai 605, a hybrid seed that gives good yield. I will not till again; we sow directly into the wheat stubble. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing, and maybe topdress with urea when the corn is knee-high. Two irrigations should be enough if the summer rain comes, but I will watch the sky. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide twice for corn borer.

I keep some grain for eating and feeding chickens, and sell the rest. I expect about 520 jin per mu for wheat and a bit more for maize if the weather is kind.

decision.reasoning_summary: I have farmed this land all my life. In Quzhou, we grow winter wheat and summer maize on the same plot every year. It is the only system I trust. I use improved wheat and hybrid maize seeds because they yield more than traditional seeds. I apply plenty of nitrogen fertilizer — I know it makes the crops green and tall. I irrigate wheat four times because it needs water through the spring, and maize twice because summer rains help. I use rotary tillage before wheat sowing, but no-tillage for maize so I can plant quickly after the wheat harvest. Pesticides are necessary to control weeds, corn borer, and wheat rust.
